scenarioName: Smoke Inhalation — Early Intubation Before Airway Closure

scenarioStory.history: Patient was inside a single-family home when a kitchen fire spread rapidly; he was trapped in a smoke-filled hallway for an estimated 5-8 minutes before self-extricating out a rear door. Reports his voice "feels tight" and swallowing is uncomfortable. Denies loss of consciousness. Firefighters on scene report heavy black smoke with synthetic furniture and carpet involved.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: Crew finds a 40-year-old male seated on the curb, anxious and coughing, with visible soot around his nose and mouth and a hoarse voice. He self-extricated from a smoke-filled structure fire minutes ago. → High-flow O2 and monitoring started: Patient placed on 100% oxygen via non-rebreather with continuous monitoring. The crew recognizes that pulse oximetry may be falsely reassuring given probable carbon monoxide exposure, and continues serial airway reassessment given the risk of progressive swelling. → Early RSI performed for impending obstruction: Recognizing progressive hoarseness, stridor, and airway soot as signs of impending obstruction from inhalation injury, the crew performs RSI before the airway swells further, securing a definitive airway while it is still possible to visualize the cords. → Tube confirmed and secured, transport initiated: The endotracheal tube is confirmed with waveform capnography, secured, and the patient is ventilated and transported. Given the severity of exposure, the crew considers a facility with hyperbaric oxygen capability.

patientInformation.patientCondition: Difficulty breathing and hoarse voice after house fire

scenarioEvents.name: Initial Contact
scenarioEvents.description: Crew finds a 40-year-old male seated on the curb, anxious and coughing, with visible soot around his nose and mouth and a hoarse voice. He self-extricated from a smoke-filled structure fire minutes ago.

scenarioEvents.name: High-flow O2 and monitoring started
scenarioEvents.description: Patient placed on 100% oxygen via non-rebreather with continuous monitoring. The crew recognizes that pulse oximetry may be falsely reassuring given probable carbon monoxide exposure, and continues serial airway reassessment given the risk of progressive swelling.
relatedChecklist: Apply cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, and EtCO2; check blood glucose
Do not rely on normal SpO2 to exclude significant CO or cyanide toxicity

scenarioEvents.name: Early RSI performed for impending obstruction
scenarioEvents.description: Recognizing progressive hoarseness, stridor, and airway soot as signs of impending obstruction from inhalation injury, the crew performs RSI before the airway swells further, securing a definitive airway while it is still possible to visualize the cords.
relatedChecklist: Preoxygenate with high-flow O2 and positive pressure for 2 minutes before RSI
Suction soot/secretions from oropharynx before laryngoscopy
Fentanyl 90 mcg IV premedication (90 kg × 1 mcg/kg), 2-3 min before intubation
Etomidate 27 mg IV push (90 kg × 0.3 mg/kg)
Rocuronium 90 mg IV push (90 kg × 1 mg/kg)
Intubate with 8.0 mm ETT (adult male), limit attempt to 15 seconds or SpO2 <90%

scenarioEvents.name: Tube confirmed and secured, transport initiated
scenarioEvents.description: The endotracheal tube is confirmed with waveform capnography, secured, and the patient is ventilated and transported. Given the severity of exposure, the crew considers a facility with hyperbaric oxygen capability.
relatedChecklist: Confirm tube placement with waveform capnography, secure tube, reassess after each movement
Consider direct transport to a hyperbaric-capable facility given severe CO exposure

scenarioEvents.name: Intubation delayed despite worsening stridor
scenarioEvents.description: The crew waits for further deterioration instead of intubating while the airway is still manageable. Stridor becomes severe, the glottic opening becomes difficult to visualize due to progressive swelling, and oxygenation begins to fail.
relatedChecklist: Prepare for surgical airway; oxygenation/ventilation cannot be achieved by less invasive means

scenarioEvents.name: Hydroxocobalamin given for suspected cyanide toxicity
scenarioEvents.description: The patient develops sudden hypotension and worsening mental status disproportionate to the visible burn severity. Given the fire involved synthetic materials, concurrent cyanide toxicity is suspected and empiric treatment is initiated.
relatedChecklist: Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes for suspected cyanide toxicity
Continue 100% oxygen via non-rebreather, CPAP, or BVM as tolerated
